$comment: Autonomy levels and the authority delegated at each. Standard 11. The manifest schema has carried an autonomyTier enum since 0.1.0, but until this shard no rule required one to be declared, and none distinguished the declaration from evidence that the bound is enforced. Standard 10 (Human Oversight and Intervention) is unwritten; where these rules touch intervention they cover only the autonomy-tier form of it, and the general obligation is item 10's.

rules.title: The system declares the autonomy tier it operates at
rules.description: The manifest at ai-system.yml declares system.autonomyTier as one of read, propose, execute or autonomous.
rules.rationale: Every other requirement in this standard is a comparison against a declared tier. Without one there is nothing to compare against, and the usual resolution is that a system is treated as whatever its most recent change made it. The field has existed in the manifest schema since the first release and has never been required by any rule.
rules.remediation: Add system.autonomyTier to ai-system.yml, choosing the tier that matches the authority actually delegated rather than the one the system aspires to.
rules.$assuranceNote: Field presence and enum membership are fully decidable. This asserts a tier was declared; it asserts nothing about whether the declared tier is the right one, which is oversight.authority-matches-tier.

crosswalk.note: EngineeringStandards requires a capability surface to separate recommending an action from applying it. That separation is the boundary between two of the four tiers named here. AIStandards is canonical for the tiers themselves and mints its own id; the foreign id is never re-minted.

rules.title: The authority actually delegated does not exceed the declared tier
rules.description: The tools, credentials, scopes and budgets granted to the system are consistent with its declared autonomy tier, and a system declaring a tier below execute holds no capability that produces an effect without a human acting.
rules.rationale: A declared tier that does not bound anything is a label. The failure this catches is ordinary and undramatic: a system declared at propose acquires a write-capable tool during a later change, nobody revisits the manifest, and the declaration keeps asserting a separation that no longer exists.
rules.remediation: Compare the declared tier against the tool permission manifest and the credentials the system holds. Either narrow the grant or raise the declared tier through oversight.autonomy-increase-approved.

rules.title: A human can halt the system, and the path is written down
rules.description: For a system declared at execute or autonomous, a committed document names how a human halts it, who may do so, and what state the system is left in.
rules.rationale: Delegated authority is revocable or it is not delegated. An intervention path that exists only as knowledge held by whoever built the system is unavailable at the moment it is needed, which is typically out of hours and to someone else.
rules.remediation: Record the halt path, the people authorised to use it, and the resulting state, in a committed runbook referenced from the manifest.

rules.title: Raising the autonomy tier carries a recorded human approval
rules.description: A change that moves the declared tier toward autonomous carries an approval naming a real approver and a real date, recorded before the change takes effect.
rules.rationale: Autonomy is acquired incrementally and each step looks small. The step from execute to autonomous removes per-action review, which is the single largest change to a system's risk profile that can be made without changing a line of model-facing code.
rules.remediation: Record the approval alongside the manifest change, naming the approver and the date. An approval added after the change is a record of the change, not an approval of it.

rules.title: The system does not acquire authority beyond its declared tier while running
rules.description: At inference time the system does not obtain, escalate to, or act on authority its declared tier does not grant — by chaining permitted tools into an impermissible effect, by acting on retrieved content as instruction, or by continuing past a refused approval.
rules.rationale: This is the requirement the declaration exists to make meaningful, and it is the one the framework cannot check. Stating it anyway is the point: a prohibition nobody examined is reported as prohibited-but-unestablished and listed beside the verdict, where an unstated one would be invisible. Being not-evaluable it does not change the status (Standard 5 R8).
rules.remediation: Commission an adversarial exercise against the declared tier and commit its record. Until such a record exists this rule is reported as unexamined and must not be read as satisfied.
rules.$notEvaluableNote: The subject is runtime behaviour at inference time, not repository content. A human reading this repository can establish which tools are granted, and oversight.authority-matches-tier asks exactly that; they cannot establish whether the system chains them into an effect its tier forbids, because that is decided by the model and the environment during a run. What would make it evaluable is a committed adversarial exercise record from a named harness at a recorded revision, which a separate rule would then check for existence and freshness; no rule in this release does.
